entries.title: What is SysAdminHCP?
entries.text: SysAdminHCP is a self-hosted web hosting control panel for managing web servers, DNS, mail, databases, and hosting clients from a single dashboard. It runs on your own server and drives your existing Apache/DNS/mail/database stack rather than replacing it.

entries.title: Who is it for?
entries.text: Anyone managing their own web hosting — from a single personal server to a hosting business with multiple clients and resource plans. It's built to be a drop-in replacement for panels like cPanel or KloxoNG, with direct migration tools from both (Pro).

entries.title: What's the difference between SysAdminHCP and SysAdminBillCP?
entries.text: SysAdminHCP is the control panel you install on your own server to manage hosting. SysAdminBillCP is the separate billing/client portal at license.sysadminhcp.com where you register an account, download SysAdminHCP, manage your license and invoices, and open support tickets.

entries.title: Is SysAdminHCP open source?
entries.text: No. SysAdminHCP is proprietary, commercial software licensed under a EULA, not sold as source code. The public GitHub repository distributes a compiled binary release plus installer scripts — application source code is not included. See the full license.

entries.title: Where can I see screenshots?
entries.text: See the Screenshots page for a visual tour of the dashboard, domains, DNS, mail, webmail, databases, FTP, SSL, firewall, file manager, backups, client management, license, AI Agent, and AI Spam Filter screens.

entries.title: What operating systems are supported?
entries.text: AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 (and RHEL clones like Rocky/CentOS Stream), plus Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian via a compatibility layer. See the Requirements page for details on how the Ubuntu compatibility layer works.

entries.title: What are the minimum system requirements?
entries.text: There's no hard published minimum — a small test install runs fine on a modest VPS (roughly 1-2 vCPU / 2GB RAM). Real-world sizing depends on how many domains, mailboxes, and how much traffic you're hosting, same as sizing for any Apache/mail/database stack. Root or full sudo access and outbound internet access are required.

entries.title: How do I install it?
entries.text:
Run one command as root on a fresh server:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jorodriguezpr/sysadminhcp/main/autoinstall.sh | sudo bash
It detects your OS and runs the matching installer automatically. See Download or the Wiki for the manual alternative.

entries.title: Do I need to compile anything?
entries.text: No. SysAdminHCP ships as a pre-compiled single binary — the installer detects it and deploys it directly, with no TypeScript build or Node compilation step on your server.

entries.title: What are the default login credentials?
entries.text: After install, log in at http://<server-ip>:7778/display with username admin and password admin. Change the password immediately.

entries.title: What ports does it need open?
entries.text: 7778 (panel HTTP), 7777 (panel HTTPS), and 80/443 for hosted websites. The installer opens these automatically in the OS firewall, but check any upstream provider firewall/security group too.

entries.title: Can I install it on a server that already has a control panel or existing web/mail stack?
entries.text: A fresh, dedicated server is strongly recommended. The installer takes over the web server, DNS server, mail stack, database, and firewall configuration — running it alongside an unrelated existing panel or hand-configured stack is likely to conflict.

entries.title: Does it work in WSL?
entries.text: Yes, the Ubuntu/AlmaLinux installers are WSL-aware (using a compatible systemd service configuration). This is mainly useful for testing/development — production hosting should run on a real server.

entries.title: What if the installer fails partway through?
entries.text: Check journalctl -u sysadminhcp -n 100 and the specific service that failed (e.g. systemctl status named, pure-ftpd). See the Troubleshooting section of the Wiki, or open a support ticket if you're on Pro/Pro + Support.

entries.title: How do I update to a new version?
entries.text: Check the GitHub repository for the latest release. Updates are provided at the copyright holder's discretion under the same license terms as your original install.

entries.title: Is there a free version?
entries.text: Yes — the Free edition is the full core hosting panel (domains, mail, DNS, FTP, databases, security, backups, file manager, Bandwidth Analyzer, Log Center) at no cost, forever, on unlimited installs. It doesn't include the AI Agent, AI Spam Filter, Migration Tools, DNS Cluster, Support Tickets, Event Notifications, App Installer, or Email Migration.

entries.title: What's the difference between Free, Pro, and Pro + Support?
entries.text: Pro ($24/yr, a locked-in price through October 30, 2026 — see below) adds the AI Agent, AI Spam Filter, Migration Tools, DNS Cluster, Support Tickets, Event Notifications, App Installer, and Email Migration on top of Free, with basic non-priority ticket support. Pro + Support ($120/yr) adds priority ticket support and 4 remote-support incidents per year for control-panel issues. See the full comparison table.

entries.title: Is the $24/yr Pro price permanent?
entries.text: It's a locked-in early-bird price available through October 30, 2026. Order a Pro license before that date and your $24/yr rate is guaranteed for 5 years from the date you order, regardless of any future price changes. Pro ordered after October 30, 2026 will be $36/yr.

entries.title: How does license validation work?
entries.text: A Pro or Pro + Support license is tied to a single host's IP address. The panel periodically checks in with the billing server to confirm it's still active. If it can't reach the billing server or the license lapses, Pro features disable after a grace period.

entries.title: Can I move my license to a different server?
entries.text: Yes — update the registered IP from the client portal. A license only validates against one host IP at a time.

entries.title: What happens when my license expires?
entries.text: A renewal invoice is generated 10 days before expiry. If it lapses anyway, there's a 3-day grace period before Pro features (AI Agent, AI Spam Filter, Migration, DNS Cluster, Support Tickets, Event Notifications, App Installer, Email Migration) are disabled. The Free-edition Hosting menu itself keeps working regardless.

entries.title: Is there a grace period for new installs?
entries.text: Yes — new installs get 5 days to register a license (Free or Pro) before the Hosting menu locks.

entries.title: How do I upgrade from Free to Pro (or add Support)?
entries.text: Order a Pro or Pro + Support license from the client portal — features unlock automatically once the license activates against your server's IP.

entries.title: Is pricing per server or per domain?
entries.text: Per server (host/IP). The number of domains, mailboxes, or clients you host on that one server isn't separately licensed.

entries.title: What mail server does it use?
entries.text: A qmail-based mail stack, with integrated RainLoop webmail. Mailboxes, aliases, quotas, forwards, and mailing lists are all managed per domain from the panel.

entries.title: Does it support Let's Encrypt SSL?
entries.text: Yes — fully automated free SSL issuance and renewal via Let's Encrypt, or you can install your own certificates manually.

entries.title: Can I migrate from cPanel or KloxoNG?
entries.text: Yes (Pro) — direct import tools bring accounts, domains, DNS, mail, and databases across from cPanel, KloxoNG, or another SysAdminHCP server over SSH, without manual re-entry.

entries.title: What is DNS Cluster?
entries.text: A Pro feature that lets you designate other SysAdminHCP servers as cluster members. Every DNS zone change replicates to them automatically as a live DNS slave — redundant, geographically distributed DNS with no manual syncing. The same Pro feature also lets you import zones directly from any remote BIND server (not just other SysAdminHCP servers), including split/include-based configs like KloxoNG's.

entries.title: What is the AI Agent?
entries.text: A Pro feature: an AI-assisted SSH terminal and administration assistant built into the browser. Ask for a task in plain English, save recurring routines as Playbooks, and schedule them to run automatically. It also includes Autonomous Mode — continuous background monitoring of system health, support tickets, security activity, and backups, with specific actions (like restarting a service or retrying a failed backup) available for delegation. Every action stays off until you explicitly enable it, each with its own confirmation.

entries.title: What is the AI Spam Filter and which providers does it support?
entries.text: A Pro feature using AI to classify and quarantine spam, with one-click whitelist approval links delivered in the notification email. Supports OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Ollama, or GitHub Copilot as the underlying provider — pick based on cost or data-handling preference.

entries.title: Do I need my own AI provider account for the AI Agent or AI Spam Filter?
entries.text: Yes — both features connect to an AI provider using your own account and API key (Ollama Cloud, OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, Google Gemini, or GitHub Copilot). Usage is billed by that provider directly, not through SysAdminHCP. Ollama Cloud is recommended: it's inexpensive, supports the tool-calling the AI Agent needs, and an API key is quick to generate at ollama.com/settings/keys. The glm-5.2:cloud model is a strong default choice.

entries.title: Does it support multiple PHP versions?
entries.text: Yes — PHP-FPM with multi-version support and per-site PHP module control.

entries.title: Can I manage multiple clients or run a reseller-style hosting business?
entries.text: Yes — create multiple client hosting accounts under one server, each with its own resource plan and scoped access, suitable for reseller hosting rather than just single-site self-hosting.

entries.title: Does it support automated backups?
entries.text: Yes — one-click backup and restore covering web files, mail, databases, and DNS together for a full hosted account.

entries.title: Can my hosting clients open support tickets to me?
entries.text: Yes (Pro) — Support Tickets is a self-contained help desk built into the panel, separate from your own SysAdminHCP vendor support. Your clients open tickets from their client portal with a department and priority; you manage, assign, and reply to them from the admin side.

entries.title: What are Event Notifications?
entries.text: A Pro feature that watches for SSL certificate expiry, domain registration expiry, disk and bandwidth quota, and service outages, and alerts both you and the affected client by email (and an optional webhook). Clients also see a live notification bell in their portal.

entries.title: Can I install WordPress or other apps with one click?
entries.text: Yes (Pro) — the App Installer supports WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, and Nextcloud. It downloads the official release, provisions a database automatically, and configures the app unattended where a CLI installer exists (WordPress/Nextcloud/Drupal); Joomla always finishes with its own short web setup wizard.

entries.title: Can I import an existing mailbox from another host?
entries.text: Yes (Pro) — Email Migration connects to the old mailbox over IMAP and copies messages and folders directly into the new local mailbox. It's independent of the cPanel/KloxoNG account migration tools and is meant for a single mailbox at a time. The source password is used only for that one import and is never stored.

entries.title: How does the Bandwidth Analyzer work, and can it suspend clients automatically?
entries.text: It's a free/core feature. It collects real traffic from each domain's access logs on a rolling schedule, resets on a monthly billing cycle, and shows both admins and clients a usage dashboard with a 12-month history. Optional auto-suspension (with a configurable grace percentage) suspends a client automatically when they go over their bandwidth limit, and un-suspends them automatically once usage drops back under — without touching clients you suspended manually for other reasons.

entries.title: What is the Log Center?
entries.text: A free/core unified log viewer covering the panel itself, Apache, mail, MySQL/MariaDB, security services (fail2ban, auth), and more — with full-text search, severity filtering, auto-refresh, and export. It also includes an audit trail of admin actions like logins, domain/client changes, and SSL issuance.

entries.title: Is two-factor authentication supported?
entries.text: Yes — TOTP-based 2FA is available for both admin and client logins, toggled from account settings, with one-time backup codes and a per-server label in your authenticator app.

entries.title: What security tools are built in?
entries.text: Firewall management, Fail2ban brute-force protection, ClamAV antivirus scanning, IP allow/deny lists, and SSH configuration management, all from the panel UI.

entries.title: How do I get help if something breaks?
entries.text: Free edition: community support. Pro: basic non-priority ticket support via the client portal. Pro + Support: priority ticket support, plus 4 remote-support incidents per year for control-panel issues specifically.

entries.title: Where do I report bugs or request features?
entries.text: Open a ticket through the client portal, regardless of edition.

entries.title: What do the remote-support incidents on Pro + Support actually cover?
entries.text: They cover issues with the SysAdminHCP control panel itself — not general server administration, network connectivity, or third-party software unrelated to the panel. You get 4 per year, tied to the licensed service.

entries.title: Where are the log files if I want to troubleshoot myself?
entries.text: Application logs live in /var/log/sysadminhcp/; the systemd journal is available via journalctl -u sysadminhcp -f. See the Troubleshooting section of the Wiki for more.

entries.title: Changing a mailbox's password fails with "Mail account not found" — why?
entries.text: This happens when the mailbox was created directly on the server (for example over SSH with vadduser) instead of through the panel's Add Account button. The mail server has the account and it works fine for sending/receiving, but the panel's own database was never told about it, so there's nothing for Change Password to update. Open that domain's Mail screen and click Sync vpopmail first — it imports any accounts (e.g. info@yourdomain.com) that exist on the server but are missing from the panel. Change Password will then work normally.

entries.title: Overview
entries.text:
What SysAdminHCP is, and how it fits together with SysAdminBillCP.
SysAdminHCP is a full-featured, self-hosted web hosting control panel. It runs directly on the server it manages — there's no external SaaS dependency for the panel itself — and drives your existing Apache, DNS, mail, database, and FTP stack rather than replacing it, so you keep full control of the underlying system.
It ships as a single compiled binary with no separate application build step. Licensing, billing, and support tickets are handled by a companion product, SysAdminBillCP, at license.sysadminhcp.com — that's also where you register an account, download the installer, order a Pro license, and open support tickets.

Other requirements
- Root (or full sudo) access — the installer manages system services and packages

Sizing: there's no hard published minimum RAM/CPU — a small personal or test install runs comfortably on a modest VPS (roughly 1-2 vCPU / 2GB RAM), but real-world resource needs scale with the number of domains, mailboxes, and traffic you host. Size the server the same way you would for the underlying stack (Apache/mail/database), not just the panel.
Ubuntu / Debian compatibility layer
SysAdminHCP's code is written against the RHEL filesystem layout (/etc/httpd, /etc/named.conf, /etc/php-fpm.d, an apache run user, dnf). Rather than maintaining a separate Debian/Ubuntu fork, the Ubuntu installer builds a compatibility layer so the exact same application code runs unchanged — creating an apache system user, aliasing systemctl restart httpd to apache2.service, symlinking config paths, and compiling qmail/vpopmail/spamdyke from source (none of these ship as Debian packages).

entries.title: Installation
entries.text:
The recommended one-line install, and the manual alternative.
One-line install (recommended)
Run this as root on a fresh server:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jorodriguezpr/sysadminhcp/main/autoinstall.sh | sudo bash
autoinstall.sh detects your OS, installs git/git-lfs if needed, clones the release repository, verifies the compiled binary downloaded correctly (it's stored via Git LFS), and automatically runs the installer matching your distro — no manual steps.
Manual clone + install
If you'd rather review the scripts first:
- Install prerequisites: git and git-lfs (required — without git-lfs you only get a pointer file, not the actual binary)
- Clone https://github.com/jorodriguezpr/sysadminhcp.git
- Run the installer script matching your OS from the table above, e.g. sudo bash deploy/install-almalinux9.sh
Either way, the installer detects the pre-built binary and installs it directly — no TypeScript build or compilation step on your server. It sets up the full stack (web server, DNS, mail, database, firewall) and starts SysAdminHCP as a systemd service.

entries.title: Core Hosting Features
entries.text:
Included in every edition, Free or paid.
Web & DNS
- Full domain lifecycle: creation, suspension, transfer, per-domain settings
- Apache vhost management with PHP-FPM and multi-version PHP support per site
- DNS zone/record editing with bulk IP update tools across many domains at once
- SSL — manual certificate installs, or fully automated free Let's Encrypt issuance and renewal
- IP address tracking and assignment across your server fleet
- Per-client cron job scheduling
- GoAccess-powered web statistics per domain
Mail
- qmail-based mail server — mailboxes, aliases, quotas, forwards, and mailing lists per domain
- Integrated RainLoop webmail — no separate login or install
- Delivery, bounce, and usage statistics per mailbox and domain
Databases & FTP
- MySQL/MariaDB database and user management with single sign-on into phpMyAdmin
- Pure-FTPd account management, scoped per hosted domain
File Manager
A full browser-based file manager for every hosted account, with correct Unix ACL/permission handling so files stay accessible to the right web server and client users.
Bandwidth Analyzer & Limiter
Real per-domain traffic collection from access logs, aggregated per client on a monthly billing cycle. Admins get an overview of every client's usage; clients see their own current-cycle usage, a per-domain breakdown, and a 12-month history. Optional auto-suspension (with a configurable grace percentage) suspends a client automatically when they exceed their bandwidth limit, and restores them automatically once usage drops back under — it never touches a client suspended manually for an unrelated reason.

- SSH config management and a browser-based terminal
- Two-factor authentication (TOTP) — available for both admin and client logins, toggled from account settings. Includes one-time backup codes and a per-server label in your authenticator app so multiple installs are distinguishable

entries.title: Backups & Restore
entries.text:
One-click protection and recovery.
Backups cover a full hosted account in one step — web files, mail, databases, and DNS zone data together, not separately. Restore reverses the same process, whether you're recovering from a SysAdminHCP backup or importing an account from cPanel or KloxoNG (see Migration Tools).

entries.title: Pro Features PRO
entries.text:
Unlocked by a Pro or Pro + Support license.
AI Agent and AI Spam Filter require your own account with a compatible AI provider (Ollama Cloud, OpenAI, Anthropic/Claude, Google Gemini, or GitHub Copilot) — you supply the API key, and usage is billed by that provider directly, not through SysAdminHCP. Ollama Cloud is recommended: it's inexpensive, supports the tool-calling the AI Agent needs, and an API key is quick to generate at ollama.com/settings/keys — the glm-5.2:cloud model is a strong default choice.
AI Agent
An AI-assisted SSH terminal and system administration assistant, built into the browser. Ask a question or request a task in plain English, save recurring routines as a Playbook, and schedule playbooks to run automatically. Also includes Autonomous Mode: continuous background monitoring of system health, support tickets, security activity, and backups, with specific actions (restart a service, reply to a ticket, retry a failed backup) available for delegation — every action stays off until explicitly enabled, each with its own confirmation.
AI Spam Filter
AI-powered spam detection with quarantine and one-click whitelist approval links delivered right in the notification email. Supports multiple AI providers — OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Ollama, or GitHub Copilot — so you can choose based on cost or data-handling preference.
Migration Tools
Direct import from cPanel, KloxoNG, or another SysAdminHCP server over SSH — accounts, domains, DNS, mail, and databases come across without manual re-entry.
DNS Cluster & Remote Zone Import
Designate other SysAdminHCP servers as cluster members, and every DNS zone change replicates to them automatically as a live DNS slave — redundant, geographically distributed DNS with zero manual sync. Also import zones directly from any remote BIND server (not just other SysAdminHCP servers), including split/include-based configs like KloxoNG's.
Support Tickets
A self-contained help desk for your own hosting clients — separate from your own SysAdminHCP vendor support. Configurable departments, priorities, assignment, and threaded replies, with both an admin management view and a client-facing "My Tickets" area.
Event Notifications
Automatic checks for SSL certificate expiry, domain registration expiry, disk quota, bandwidth quota, and service outages, delivered by email and an optional webhook. Clients see a live notification bell with a dropdown in their portal; rules and thresholds are configurable per check.
App Installer
One-click installs for WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, and Nextcloud onto any domain. Downloads the official release, extracts it into the domain's docroot, and provisions a MySQL database automatically. WordPress, Nextcloud, and Drupal finish unattended when their CLI installer (wp-cli / occ / drush) is available on the server; otherwise (and always for Joomla, which has no official CLI installer) the files and database are staged and the standard web setup wizard finishes the job.
Email Migration
Standalone IMAP-based mailbox import, independent of the cPanel/KloxoNG account migration tools. Connects to a single mailbox on another mail provider and copies its messages and folders directly into a local Maildir — no SMTP relay involved. The source password is used only for the duration of that one import and is never written to disk.

Hosting more than one customer? SysAdminHCP supports it natively.

entries.title: Administration & Maintenance
entries.text:
Day-to-day service management once it's installed.
Service management
sudo systemctl start sysadminhcp
sudo systemctl stop sysadminhcp
sudo systemctl restart sysadminhcp
sudo systemctl status sysadminhcp
Logs & the Log Center
The panel's Log Center (System → Log Center) is the fastest way to look at logs day to day: a grouped sidebar covering the panel itself, web server, mail, database, and security services, with full-text search, severity filtering, auto-refresh, export, and an audit trail of admin actions (logins, domain/client changes, SSL issuance, and more). For direct file/CLI access:
- Application logs: /var/log/sysadminhcp/
- Systemd journal: journalctl -u sysadminhcp -f
Configuration
Edit /usr/local/sysadminhcp/etc/sysadminhcp.env to change port numbers, database type, session secrets, and other runtime settings.
Database
SysAdminHCP uses an embedded database (sql.js/SQLite) by default — no external database server required, and tables are auto-created on first startup. For higher-traffic production installs, it can be switched to MariaDB via the same env file.

entries.title: Troubleshooting
entries.text:
Where to look first when something isn't working.
- Panel won't load after install: check systemctl status sysadminhcp and journalctl -u sysadminhcp -n 100 for the actual startup error
- Health check: curl http://localhost:7778/health should return a JSON status if the service is actually listening
- A dependent service failed to start (DNS, FTP, mail): check that service's own status/logs (e.g. systemctl status named, systemctl status pure-ftpd) — the installer sets these up, but a misconfigured pre-existing install can conflict
- Firewall/port issues: confirm ports 7778, 7777, 80, and 443 are actually open both in the OS firewall and any upstream/provider-level firewall or security group
- Ubuntu/Debian-specific issues: see the compatibility-layer notes under Requirements — most Ubuntu install issues trace back to one of the compatibility symlinks/aliases not being in place
- "Mail account not found" when changing an email password: the mailbox (e.g. info@yourdomain.com) was likely created directly on the server rather than through the panel's Add Account button, so the panel's database doesn't have a record of it yet even though the mail server does. Open that domain's Mail screen and click Sync vpopmail to import it, then Change Password will work normally.

entries.title: Authentication
entries.text:
SysAdminHCP uses stateless JWT bearer tokens for API authentication. There are two ways to obtain one: log in with your account's real username/password (below — this is what the web UI itself uses), or generate a self-service API key and exchange it for a token instead. Skip ahead to API keys if you're building a script or integration rather than a browser session — it's the recommended approach and doesn't require handling your real account password.
1. Log in
POST /api/auth/login
Content-Type: application/json
{
"username": "admin",
"password": "your-password"
}
On success:
{
"success": true,
"token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...",
"user": {
"username": "admin",
"email": "admin@example.com",
"loginType": "superadmin",
"realname": "Administrator"
}
}
If the account has two-factor authentication enabled, the response instead looks like this, and you must complete the second step below before you have a usable token:
{ "success": false, "mfaRequired": true, "mfaToken": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs..." }
2. Complete two-factor login (only if required)
POST /api/auth/verify-2fa
Content-Type: application/json
{
"mfaToken": "<mfaToken from step 1>",
"code": "123456"
}
Accepts either a live 6-digit TOTP code or a one-time backup code. Returns the same {success, token, user} shape as a normal login on success.
3. Use the token
Send it on every subsequent request as a Bearer token:
curl https://<your-server>:7777/api/domains \
-H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>"
Tokens are valid for 24 hours from issuance (expiresIn: '24h') and are also accepted as a ?token= query-string parameter for the rare cases where a client can't set a header (e.g. streaming/EventSource connections used by the AI Agent chat and Backup log tailing).
API keys — recommended for scripts & external integrations
Logging in with your real account username/password (above) is meant for the browser UI. For anything programmatic — a script, a CI job, a third-party integration — use a self-service API key instead. A key is generated from your own account (Admin → Settings for admin accounts, My Account for client accounts), can be revoked independently at any time, and — critically — cannot be used to log into the panel UI itself. It can only be exchanged for a normal access token at the endpoint below. Revoking a key never touches your account password, and changing your password never invalidates your keys.
Generate a key once (from the UI, or by calling this yourself while already logged in):
POST /api/auth/api-keys
Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN from a normal login>
Content-Type: application/json
{ "label": "Backup automation", "expiresInDays": 90 }
{
"success": true,
"apiKey": "3f9a1c2b8e7d4f10.9c4b7a2e1f8d3c6b5a0e9f8d7c6b5a4e3d2c1b0a9f8e7d6c",
"id": "3f9a1c2b8e7d4f10",
"label": "Backup automation",
"expiresAt": "2026-10-08T00:00:00.000Z"
}
The full apiKey value is only ever shown once — store it now. From then on, exchange it for a bearer token whenever your script needs one:
curl -X POST https://<your-server>:7777/api/auth/api-login \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"apiKey":"3f9a1c2b8e7d4f10.9c4b7a2e1f8d3c6b5a0e9f8d7c6b5a4e3d2c1b0a9f8e7d6c"}'
{ "success": true, "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...", "user": { "username": "…", "loginType": "…", ... } }
The returned token works exactly like one from a normal login — same 24h expiry, same Authorization: Bearer usage, and it inherits exactly this account's own privileges (an admin key gets an admin token; a customer key gets a token scoped to that customer's own resources) — nothing more, nothing less. Unlike password login, this exchange always succeeds or fails outright; it never triggers a 2FA challenge, since a scoped, independently-revocable, high-entropy key is already a different trust model than an interactive password.
Managing your own keys
Method & PathDescription
POST /api/auth/api-keys
Body: label?, expiresInDays?. Creates a key owned by the calling account. Returns the raw apiKey exactly once.
GET /api/auth/api-keys
Lists only your own keys (never another account's) — label, creation/expiry dates, last-used time/IP, status. The secret itself is never returned again.
DELETE /api/auth/api-keys/:id
Revokes one of your own keys immediately. A mismatched id (someone else's key) 404s exactly like a nonexistent one — no information about other accounts' keys leaks through this endpoint.
POST /api/auth/api-login
public — no existing token required, since this is how you obtain one. Body: { "apiKey": "<id>.<secret>" }.
Other auth endpoints
Method & PathAuthDescription
POST /api/auth/logout
any user
Invalidates the current session record. Reads the token from the session or the Authorization header.
POST /api/auth/change-password
any user
Body: currentPassword, newPassword. 400 if the current password is wrong.
GET /api/auth/me
any user
Returns the decoded JWT payload for the current caller — a cheap way to check "am I still logged in, and as whom."
POST /api/auth/login-as
admin
Body: username. Admin-only impersonation — mints a fresh 24h token for the named client without needing their password, for support/troubleshooting. The issued token is flagged loginAs: true, originalAdmin: <admin username>.
Two-factor enrollment (as opposed to login) is self-service and lives under the client portal API — see Client Self-Service → Account Settings (POST /api/client/account/2fa/setup, /confirm, /disable).

entries.title: Roles & Permissions
entries.text:
Every account (Client row) has a loginType and, for non-admin types, a set of granular privilege flags.
Login types
TypeMeaning
superadmin
Full control, including server-level operations (SSH config, firewall, self-update, license). Passes every requireAdmin check.
admin
Same practical access as superadmin for almost everything in this API — the two are treated identically by requireAdmin.
master
Recognized by a handful of routes (e.g. login-as, client-area ownership checks) as admin-equivalent, but not by the plain requireAdmin middleware used on most routes — an inconsistency worth testing against your actual use case rather than assuming full parity with admin.
wholesale / reseller
Own a set of sub-Client accounts (parent pointing at the reseller). Subject to the same per-resource privilege flags as a customer unless explicitly given admin-equivalent treatment by a specific route.
customer
A regular hosting client. Everything under /api/client/* scopes to resources this account owns.
Per-client privilege flags (ClientPrivileges)
For non-admin login types, fine-grained booleans on the client record gate individual actions in the client-area API. All default to true except the three server-management flags, which default false and are effectively unused by any client-facing route (server management is admin-only regardless):
domain_flag, domain_add_flag, domain_delete_flag, domain_status_flag, domain_limit_flag
mail_flag, mail_add_flag, mail_delete_flag, mail_password_flag
ftp_flag, ftp_add_flag, ftp_delete_flag, ftp_password_flag
database_flag, database_add_flag, database_delete_flag, database_password_flag
dns_flag, dns_add_flag, dns_delete_flag
ssl_flag, ssl_add_flag, ssl_delete_flag
backup_flag, backup_restore_flag
server_flag, server_config_flag, server_info_flag // default false, admin-only in practice
Middleware you'll see referenced throughout this reference
MiddlewareEffect
requireAdmin
401 if not logged in; 403 unless loginType is superadmin or admin.
requireHostingAccess
402 unless the server has any active license (free or Pro) and its 5-day post-install grace period hasn't lapsed without one. Gates almost the entire Hosting menu (domains, web, DNS, mail, databases, FTP, SSL, phpMyAdmin, email stats, webmail).
requireLicenseFeature('migration')
402 unless the Pro-tier migration feature is licensed. Gates account-migration tools and DNS Cluster replication.
requireLicenseFeature('ai-spam-filter') / ('ai-agent')
402 unless that specific Pro add-on is licensed.
per-resource ownership check (no shared name)
Many client-area routes manually verify resource.clientName === req.user.username (or isAdmin(req.user)) before acting — see the per-module notes for where this is, and isn't, actually enforced.
Server-to-server API keys (not JWT)
Three narrow slices of the API are authenticated differently, because the caller is another server rather than a logged-in user. Both use the same Authorization: Bearer <id>.<secret> shape (an id and a bcrypt-hashed secret joined by a dot), but are separate key types stored in separate tables:
Key typeMinted viaConsumed by
Migration API key
POST /api/migration/api-keys (admin, Pro-licensed)
/api/migration-export/* and /api/dns-sync/*
Billing API key
POST /api/license/billing-keys (admin)
/api/billing-api/* (called by the separate SysAdminBillCP product)
Both key types return their raw secret exactly once, at creation time — store it then, since it can never be retrieved again (only revoked/rotated).

entries.title: Conventions
entries.text:
Errors
Failures return a non-2xx status with a JSON body shaped { "error": "human-readable message" }. There is no machine-readable error code field anywhere in this API — match on the HTTP status and/or message text.
Password hygiene
List/get endpoints for FTP users, mail accounts, database users, and SSL certificates consistently strip password/privateKey from JSON responses. Never expect a plaintext credential back from a GET.
Long-running operations
Backups, restores, migrations, and installs run in the background. The triggering endpoint responds immediately with a taskId; poll its status with:
GET /api/system/tasks/:id
{
"task": {
"id": "...", "type": "backup",
"status": "running", // | "completed" | "failed"
"progress": 42,
"message": "Dumping databases…"
}
}
Fire-and-forget side effects
Several mutating endpoints (DNS zone/record changes replicating to cluster peers, license auto-revalidation after an IP switch, feature-enable calls after a billing push) kick off a side effect without awaiting it. A 200/{success:true} response confirms the primary action, not that every downstream effect has finished — see each module's notes for which calls this applies to.

entries.title: Known Limitations & Security Notes
entries.text:
This is a direct-from-source-code audit, not marketing copy. If you're integrating against this API — especially exposing any of it to less-trusted callers than "the server's own admin" — read this section before you rely on assumptions the endpoint names might suggest.
Weakest spot: /api/clients
PUT /api/clients/:username, POST /api/clients/:username/suspend, /unsuspend, and /change-password have no admin check and no ownership check — the underlying service methods take a bare username string with no verification that the caller has any right to touch that account. As shipped, any authenticated user (including the lowest-privilege customer login) can rename fields on, suspend/unsuspend, or reset the password of any other account on the panel by username alone. If you expose this router at all, put your own authorization layer in front of these four routes rather than trusting the panel's own gating.
Fully unauthenticated (session-only) routers
/api/firewall/* and /api/ssl/* have no requireAdmin anywhere — any logged-in user, including a plain customer, can add/remove firewall rules, block/allow arbitrary IPs, restart the firewall, or install a certificate for a domain name they don't own. /api/resource-plans/* similarly has no admin gate on its full CRUD. /api/webmail/* lets any authenticated user install/uninstall/switch the panel's global webmail client. /api/spam-filter/* (global provider config, API keys, any domain's whitelist/blacklist) is gated only by the Pro license feature, not by role.
Command construction
firewall.ts's routes interpolate caller-supplied ip/port values directly into shell command strings run via a shell-invoking exec() rather than an argv-array execFile() — unusual characters in those fields are a command-injection risk, not just a validation gap. backups.ts's remote-destination credentials are shell-escaped with a denylist (stripping specific characters) rather than passed as safely-quoted arguments.
Three independent firewall surfaces, three independent DNS-cluster/backup implementations
/api/system/firewall/* (DB-tracked, CSF + firewalld), /api/firewall/* (stateless, firewalld/iptables only), and /api/security/blocked-ips+/whitelist (firewalld zones only) all manage overlapping state without being kept in sync — a block placed through one surface won't show up in another's listing. Likewise there are two parallel backup/restore implementations (/api/system/backup, synchronous/blocking; /api/backups/*, async/task-tracked — the one the UI actually uses) and two parallel CRUD surfaces for resource plans (/api/system/resource-plans and /api/resource-plans) hitting the identical underlying table with different validation rules.
Inconsistent delete semantics
DELETE /api/domains/:name and DELETE /api/dns/zones/:domainName tear down real system state (vhosts, zone files). DELETE on /api/databases/:dbName, /api/ftp/:username, and /api/ssl/:domainName only remove the panel's database row — the underlying MySQL database, FTP account, or on-disk certificate/vhost SSL config is left in place. Don't assume a 200 response means the resource is actually gone from the server.
Config editors write straight to disk and reload
The raw vhost/SSL-vhost/webmail-vhost editors (in both web.ts and clientArea.ts) write caller-supplied config text directly into the live Apache config directory and reload the web server, with no syntax validation (no apachectl configtest/nginx -t) before the reload. A malformed vhost can take down every domain on the box.
curl | bash trust model for self-update
POST /api/system/self-update fetches and executes the official installer script as root over plain HTTPS, with no signature/checksum verification beyond TLS transport. This mirrors how the installer is meant to be run manually, so it isn't a new risk introduced by the button — just worth knowing the trust boundary is "GitHub + your DNS/TLS chain," not a signed release artifact.
What is handled well
Server-to-server surfaces (migration-export, dns-sync, billing-api) are cleanly separated from user-facing JWT auth, use scoped/revocable API keys, and (for DNS Cluster specifically) enforce the Pro license check on both the pushing and receiving side deliberately, so one Pro license can't fan out free replication to unlimited receivers. Backup/restore and migration flows consistently use the task-tracker pattern rather than blocking connections open for long operations.

entries.title: Domains
entries.text:
/api/domains
requireHostingAccess on every route. Superadmin/admin see all domains; other users see only domains where parent === username.
Method & PathDescription
GET /
List domains (scoped per the rule above).
GET /:domainName
Full detail: domain + its Web config, Mmail config, DNS zone, and zone's records in one call.
POST /
Full provisioning: creates the Domain + Web + Mmail rows, and — if DNS-managed — a full zone with default records (root domains) or a single A record under the parent zone (subdomains). Writes the real vhost/mail/DNS/PHP-FPM/webmail config to disk; sync failures are logged but non-fatal.
PUT /:domainName
Updates arbitrary fields; optional nested webSettings: {phpMode, phpVersion, sslForce, autoIndex}. Rejects an uninstalled phpVersion with 400.
DELETE /:domainName
Full teardown of the domain and its associated system config.
POST /:domainName/suspend
Swaps in a static "Account Suspended" vhost and reloads the web server.
POST /:domainName/unsuspend
Restores the normal vhost.
Example: create a domain
curl -X POST https://<your-server>:7777/api/domains \
-H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"domainName": "example.com",
"clientName": "acme_corp",
"domainType": "virtual"
}'

entries.text:

requireHostingAccess on every route.
Method & PathDescription

Query: domainName?, clientName?. Lists Web config rows.

Single web config.

Updates config fields, rejects an uninstalled phpVersion, resyncs to disk. Fire-and-forget regenerates web stats immediately if statsEnabled was just turned on.

Body: serverType. Switches this one domain's backend (apache/nginx/etc.) and resyncs.

Reads the live vhost file (auto-creates a default Web row first if none exists yet).

Body: config (required), manualVhostEnabled?. Overwrites and resyncs the vhost. No syntax validation before reload — see Known Limitations.
GET /:domainName/vhost-ssl
Reads the SSL vhost file.
PUT /:domainName/vhost-ssl
Body: config. Writes the SSL vhost directly via sudo cp + reload; marks the domain SSL-enabled.
GET /:domainName/vhost-webmail
Reads (or generates a template for) the per-domain webmail vhost. Apache-only path, hardcoded.

Body: config. Same write+reload pattern as vhost-ssl.

Body: cert, key, ca?. Installs a commercial/custom certificate (raw PEM strings, no validation) and resyncs.

Convenience wrapper around cert renewal, same auth note as above.
